news.title: USPSTF Members Concerned About Changes As AHRQ Boosts AI Use
news.description: Body: As the U.S. Preventative Services Task Force convened Thursday (Nov. 19) for the first time in over a year, and the first time since HHS Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. added new members and granted them unusual conflict-of-interest waivers, former members raised concerns the administration’s plan to deeply incorporate generative artificial intelligence in USPSTF’s work coupled with the invited “experts” presentations could undermine the group’s neutrality. USPSTF began its two-day meeting by hearing presentations Thursday on cervical cancer screening, screening and counseling for alcohol use in adolescents and adults, perinatal depression counseling and prevention, and lifestyle modifications to prevent cardiovascular disease. Members’ conflicts of interest were noted several times, though no votes were taken. Several of the presentations were drafted in 2024, with members noting USTSPF has been blocked from meeting in the intervening time. USPSTF recommendations on at least 18 topics have been stalled since the Task Force last met in May 2025. On Friday, the panel will hear presentations on screening for chronic kidney disease, colorectal cancer and lung cancer. HHS has not confirmed when votes on the topics will be taken or when the results will be made public. The Affordable Care Act requires preventive care recommended by USPSTF with an “A” or “B” grade be covered by most private health plans and some Medicaid plans. Medical stakeholders were already concerned that Kennedy’s additions to USPSTF included specialists and a health care finance expert, while its membership has usually consisted of primary care doctors and other general practitioners. Further alarms were raised by reporting that all eight of Kennedy’s new members received conflict-of-interest waivers to participate in the Task Force, despite at least four holding stock in pharmaceutical companies. The American College of Preventive Medicine said in a recent statement it “urges that appropriate safeguards be put into place to ensure evidence-based, prevention-focused recommendations prevail to the benefit of the American people.” Sens. Angus King (I-ME) and Elizabeth Warren (D-MA) were motivated by the appointments to introduce legislation barring conflicts of interest on USPSTF. Ron Klein, director of the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, which oversees USPSTF, noted that Thursday’s meeting that financial conflicts of interest are permissible because of the Supreme Court decision last year that members of the Task Force are HHS “inferior officers.” The case, Kennedy v. Braidwood Management, Inc., allowed the HHS secretary to override USPSTF’s recommendations. But observers have noted the COI waivers clash with Kennedy’s promises of a zero-tolerance policy for corporate influence at HHS. More attention was drawn to USPSTF Wednesday (Nov. 18) by a New York Times report that Klein wants to use artificial intelligence for the task force’s evidence reviews, which Klein confirmed Thursday. Klein said he felt AI had been used to write “a lot of” the material presented at the meeting Thursday, though others at the virtual meeting said AI had not been used. Klein did not go into detail on the use of AI he wanted at Thursday’s meeting. The New York Times reported he had suggested dropping the Task Force’s established expert review process and instead having his assistant complete reviews with AI. On Friday, USPSTF is set to hear from “subject matter experts” on chronic kidney disease, colorectal cancer and lung cancer, though the meeting agenda does not specify who the experts are. Several members of the panel predating Kennedy said they were concerned the presentations would filter evidence through a single individual’s viewpoint and be perceived as attempts to influence the viewpoints of Task Force members, shifting further away from its usual process of evidence compilation and review. Task Force member Sei Lee said the subject matter experts could provide more information published research has not yet caught up to, but cautioned the presentations risked giving one interpretation of evidence more prominence than the systemic review process. Member Joel Tsevat said the introduction of subject matter expert presentations could become an infringement on the group’s scientific independence. “We heard at the September orientation the HHS deputy general counsel explained what scientific independence means following the Braidwood Supreme Court decision, and I quote, he said it means being independent from outside pressure. And these presentations seem to me to be trying to persuade the task force to expedite review of these topics and make recommendations regarding specific screening modalities, and so in my view, these constitute outside pressure, and then therefore, for the first time in the history of the task force, infringe on our scientific independence,” Tsevat said. Tsevat said public confidence in the Task Force’s review process would be undermined if it is perceived as being more likely to act on topics that are presented on at a public meeting. “Not to say that on top of that, this that session is taking up over a third of our meeting time, and I wonder if we could use that time in the future more efficiently by reviewing, deliberating on systematic evidence reviews and Task Force draft recommendations,” he added. -- Jessica Karins (jkarins@iwpnews.com)

news.title: Navy under secretary nominee wants a new foreign-backed domestic shipyard for frigate production
news.description: The United States should support the creation of a new domestic shipyard backed by foreign investment to build frigates, Navy under secretary nominee William Toti told lawmakers today following congressional pushback on a Trump administration plan to build warships overseas. Addressing the Senate Armed Services Committee during a confirmation hearing today, Toti said he views establishing a new domestic yard focused on frigate production as the fastest way to fill a fleet capability gap and expand the nation’s warship inventory towards its 355-vessel requirement. “We have destroyers today doing frigate work, and the quickest way to get frigates in the United States Navy is to establish a new shipyard, world-class shipyard, that’s focused just on those ships,” he said. “The best way to do that, in my understanding, in all the analysis that I have done, is to get a foreign shipyard who does world-class work right now to invest in the United States with a new shipyard that focuses just on those ships.” A new greenfield yard backed by foreign capital and know-how could expand production capacity, he continued, saying Korean and Japanese shipbuilders are the best in the world from a production standpoint, and can help strengthen the U.S. industrial base. Toti’s remarks came in response to questions from Sen. Angus King (ME), who criticized the administration’s earlier push to begin building a surface combatant using the “Finland model,” under which foreign shipbuilders would construct initial vessels overseas while preparing U.S. yards for follow-on work. The proposal has been largely rejected by Congress, with both the House and Senate advancing draft legislation that would block portions of the plan as it applies to warships. Lawmakers may allow the Pentagon to apply this approach to non-combatant auxiliary vessels. Today, King also criticized the Navy’s decision to include only one Arleigh Burke-class destroyer in its fiscal year 2027 budget request. Along with this reduction, the Navy proposed building a destroyer in Japan and a frigate in Korea, according to King. In response to King’s questions, Toti said he is “no longer on the bandwagon of building ships in foreign shipyards,” but added, “let me make sure I’m clear on what that means.” Toti went on to say he supports foreign shipbuilders investing in domestic facilities. It was unclear whether he still supports the original proposal that would see initial warships built in foreign yards. Toti previously performed the duties of Navy under secretary starting in May. However, he stepped down from this role on Sept. 14 when he was nominated for the position in an official capacity, so his remarks today don't necessarily represent the Navy’s position on the issue. On Friday, days before a series of confirmation hearings for Navy officials including Toti and acting Navy Secretary Hung Cao, a service spokesperson told Inside Defense that the Pentagon and Navy had not yet delivered a White House-directed plan to begin building ships in foreign yards -- reversing a prior statement that confirmed the plan’s delivery a day earlier. An Aug. 13 national security memorandum from President Trump gave the defense and Navy secretaries 90 days to develop and deliver competitive acquisition programs for a Navy surface combatant and two auxiliary ships in line with the Finland Model. Although this plan was due Nov. 12, it has not yet been delivered, the service spokesperson said Friday. Today, King appeared satisfied with Toti’s answers for the time being. “If you’re talking about investing in the United States, that’s different than building overseas. We’ll continue this discussion,” he said.
